results.result: Homeostatic synaptic plasticity of mEPSC amplitude is impaired in cortical cultures from Rab3a−/− and Rab3aEbd/Ebd mice. TTX treatment increased mEPSC amplitude in wild-type cultures (13.9±0.7 to 18.2±0.9 pA, p=0.007), but not in Rab3a−/− cultures (13.6±0.1 vs 14.3±0.6 pA, p=0.998) or Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures (15.1±1.0 vs 14.6±1.1 pA, p=0.81).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C20, C21, C24, C26, and C29 provide converging electrophysiological evidence from two independent genetic models (knockout and point mutant) showing impaired homeostatic plasticity. The data include appropriate sample sizes (20-30 cells per condition), statistical tests (two-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc), and consistent results across multiple cultures (11 cultures for Rab3a−/−, 6-7 for Rab3aEbd/Ebd).

results.result: Rab3a acts in neurons, not glia, to mediate homeostatic plasticity. Glial feeder layer experiments showed that mEPSC amplitude increased when Rab3a was present in neurons (WT on WT: 13.3±0.5 to 16.7±1.2 pA; WT on KO: 13.3±1.0 to 18.8±1.4 pA), but not when Rab3a was present only in glia (KO on WT: 15.2±1.1 to 16.9±0.7 pA).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C69, C70, C73, C74, and C75 demonstrate through cell-type-specific manipulation that neuronal Rab3a is necessary for homeostatic plasticity. The glial feeder layer approach provides appropriate controls (WT on WT, WT on KO, KO on WT) to distinguish neuronal from glial contributions, with statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc) supporting the conclusions.

results.result: The TTX-induced increase in mEPSC amplitude does not depend on Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors. NASPM application did not reverse the TTX effect on amplitude (pre-NASPM: CON 12.9±3.5 pA, TTX 17.5±3.1 pA; post-NASPM: CON 11.9±2.6 pA, TTX 16.1±3.5 pA), ruling out contribution of GluA1, GluA3, GluA4 homomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40, C44, and C98 provide pharmacological evidence using NASPM to exclude Ca2+-permeable receptors. The within-cell design (paired measurements before/after NASPM, n=11 cells) is appropriate, and the statistical analysis (paired t-test) is correctly applied. The modest reduction in amplitude by NASPM validates drug efficacy without affecting the TTX-induced increase.

results.result: GluA2 receptor cluster size showed a trend toward increase after TTX treatment (18.1%) similar in magnitude to mEPSC amplitude increase (19.7%), but did not reach statistical significance in pooled data from 3 or 5 cultures. In Rab3a−/− cultures, neither mEPSC amplitude nor GluA2 receptor levels increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60, C99-C101 report immunofluorescence data that trends in the expected direction but lacks statistical significance (p=0.21 for 5 cultures). The authors acknowledge high variability (C101) and smaller sample sizes for imaging (~20 synapses/dendrite) compared to electrophysiology. While the magnitude of change is similar to mEPSC amplitude, the lack of significance prevents definitive conclusions about receptor contribution.

results.result: TTX treatment increased mEPSC frequency in wild-type cultures from the Rab3a+/− colony (2.26±0.37 to 4.62±0.74 s−1, p=0.09), but this increase was reduced in Rab3a−/− cultures (2.74±0.49 to 3.23±0.93 s−1, p=0.999). The frequency effect was less consistent across wild-type strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C23, C27, and C28 report frequency changes that are less robust and consistent than amplitude changes. The p-value for the WT frequency increase (p=0.09) does not reach significance, and the effect varies between wild-type strains. The presence of outliers in Rab3a−/− cultures (C23) and baseline differences in Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures (C28) complicate interpretation.

results.result: Baseline mEPSC amplitudes differ between genotypes: Rab3a−/− cultures show normal baseline amplitudes indistinguishable from wild-type (13.6±0.1 vs 13.9±0.7 pA), while Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures show significantly elevated baseline amplitudes (15.1±1.0 vs 11.0±0.7 pA, p=0.04).
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C31, and C118 document important baseline differences between genetic models. The statistical comparison (two-way ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc) appropriately identifies the significant elevation in Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures while confirming normal baseline in Rab3a−/− cultures. This phenotypic difference between knockout and point mutant is well-documented with adequate sample sizes.

results.result: VGLUT1 levels at presynaptic sites did not increase after TTX treatment. In Rab3a+/+ cultures, VGLUT1 size was unchanged with trends toward reduced intensity and integral. Similar lack of change was observed in Rab3a−/− cultures.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 and C90-C92 provide consistent negative results for VGLUT1 changes across genotypes, supported by quantitative measurements (Table 2) and comparison with prior literature (C91). The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations (cannot rule out simultaneous vesicle number reduction, C62) and correctly conclude lack of evidence for VGLUT1 contribution to homeostatic plasticity.

results.result: NASPM reduced mEPSC frequency more in TTX-treated cultures (4.40±3.51 to 2.68±2.25 s−1) than control cultures (1.84±0.55 to 1.56±0.53 s−1), suggesting activity blockade may promote synaptic sites containing only Ca2+-permeable receptors, though these sites do not contribute to amplitude increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 propose a mechanism for NASPM's frequency effect based on the differential magnitude of reduction between control and TTX conditions. However, this interpretation is speculative (C41, C42 marked as SPECULATION), and the high variability in TTX frequency measurements (SD of 3.51 s−1) weakens confidence. The conclusion that these sites don't contribute to amplitude (C43) is more solid, based on Figure 3A data.

results.result: Baseline mEPSC amplitudes differed between the two wild-type strains (13.9±0.7 pA for Rab3a+/− colony vs 11.0±0.6 pA for Rab3a+/Ebd colony), but this difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.27).
results.evaluation: Claim C25 documents an important methodological consideration about genetic background differences between colonies. The statistical test (Tukey comparison after two-way ANOVA) is appropriate, and the authors transparently report the numerical difference while correctly noting lack of statistical significance. This affects interpretation of cross-colony comparisons.

results.result: Alternative statistical analysis using individual synaptic sites as sample size (6 sites/cell) yielded highly significant p-values for GluA2 changes (p=0.001 for 3 cultures, p=0.005 for 5 cultures). Comparison with literature suggests receptor measurements are more variable than mEPSC amplitude measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 present an alternative analysis that achieves significance by inflating sample size (treating individual synapses as independent), which violates statistical independence assumptions since multiple synapses come from the same cell/culture. While the comparison with Xu & Pozzo-Miller (C105) supports greater variability in receptor measurements, the alternative analysis approach is methodologically questionable and the authors appropriately did not use it as their primary analysis.

results.result: The lack of statistically significant increase in GluA2 receptor levels leaves open the possibility of a presynaptic contribution to quantal size, though technical variability in immunofluorescence cannot be ruled out. The site of Rab3a action (pre- vs postsynaptic) remains uncertain without compartment-specific deletion experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 appropriately acknowledge the limitations of the current data and the multiple possible interpretations. The authors correctly note that without significant receptor changes, presynaptic mechanisms remain possible (C107), while also acknowledging alternative explanations (C108) and the need for additional experiments (C110). This represents appropriate scientific caution given the data.

results.result: Loss of Rab3a in glia did not disrupt homeostatic plasticity, making it unlikely that Rab3a acts via the astrocytic-TNFα pathway. Previous work showed normal homeostatic plasticity at the NMJ in TNFα−/− mice, suggesting Rab3a may act via a non-TNFα mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 integrate current glial feeder layer results (C115) with prior NMJ findings (C116) to argue against the TNFα pathway. The logic is sound: if Rab3a in glia were required for TNFα release, then WT neurons on KO glia should show impaired plasticity, but they don't (C69-C70). The citation to prior work (C116) strengthens the argument for TNFα-independent mechanisms.

results.result: The elevated baseline mEPSC amplitude in Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures could reflect either occlusion of homeostatic plasticity (if there's a ceiling effect) or the mutant protein mimicking activity blockade. Similar phenotypes in other deletion mutants suggest a possible general phenomenon where disrupted homeostatic regulation causes elevated baseline amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C124 present two competing interpretations of the Earlybird phenotype, both speculative. The occlusion hypothesis (C119) is weakened by the lack of elevated baseline in Rab3a−/− cultures (C122), while the mimicry hypothesis (C124) lacks direct mechanistic evidence. The comparison with other mutants (C120-C121) is interesting but doesn't definitively support either interpretation. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish these possibilities.

results.result: One interpretation is that Rab3a is required for an increase in the presynaptic quantum in both NMJ and cortical neurons. Possible mechanisms include modulation of fusion pore kinetics or activity-dependent increases in vesicle size, though the latter would require only ~3% diameter increase and be difficult to detect.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C88, and C97 are explicitly speculative (marked as INFERENCE/SPECULATION). While the interpretation integrates NMJ and cortical data, it remains hypothetical without direct evidence for presynaptic quantum changes in cortical cultures. The proposed mechanisms (fusion pore, vesicle size) are plausible based on prior work but lack direct experimental support in the current study.

results.result: This is the first demonstration that a presynaptic protein (Rab3a) is required for homeostatic synaptic plasticity of quantal size in central neurons, representing a novel finding in the field.
results.evaluation: Claims C8 and C127 assert novelty based on the authors' knowledge of the literature. However, the claim is complicated by the uncertain mechanism of Rab3a action (C110) - if Rab3a acts postsynaptically on receptor trafficking, the novelty claim would be undermined. The claim would be more strongly supported with compartment-specific deletion experiments confirming presynaptic action.

results.result: Immunofluorescence methodology focused on primary apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons, where glutamate sensitivity increases after activity blockade. Analysis averaged ~20 synaptic pairs per dendrite (range 11-38), with synapses located 38.5±2.8 μm from soma in control and 42.4±3.2 μm in TTX-treated cells (p=0.35).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 and C51 describe methodological details that are well-documented with appropriate justification (C46 cites prior work showing increased glutamate response in this region). The quantification of synapse number (C47) and distance from soma (C51) with statistical comparison demonstrates rigor. The lack of distance difference between conditions (p=0.35) appropriately controls for potential location-dependent effects.

results.result: Culture-to-culture variability in receptor response was observed: 3/3 cultures showed increased mEPSC amplitude, but only 2/3 showed increased GluA2 cluster size (one showed decrease). Additional cultures and GluA1 measurements confirmed inconsistent receptor increases despite robust mEPSC amplitude increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 document important variability in the receptor measurements across independent cultures. The culture-by-culture analysis (Figure 5A-C) transparently shows the inconsistency, and the GluA1 data (C55) confirms the issue is not specific to GluA2. This variability is a key finding that motivates the authors' cautious interpretation and is well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: In glial feeder layer cultures, Rab3a−/− neurons showed a trend toward elevated baseline mEPSC amplitude (15.2±1.1 vs 13.3±0.5 pA, p=0.78) and frequency (4.46±1.21 vs 2.54±0.57 s−1, p=0.59), though neither reached significance. Frequency trends differed between genotypes after TTX treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C71 and C72 report baseline differences in the glial feeder layer experiments with appropriate statistical tests (Tukey post-hoc after two-way ANOVA). The authors correctly note the trends without overclaiming significance. These observations parallel the elevated baseline in Rab3aEbd/Ebd dissociated cultures (C31), suggesting some consistency in phenotype, though the lack of significance limits strong conclusions.

results.result: Smaller sample sizes in imaging experiments (limited to primary dendrites) and technical complexity of immunofluorescence processing may contribute to greater variability in receptor measurements compared to electrophysiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C102 and C103 provide reasonable explanations for the observed variability. The sample size limitation (C102) is documented with appropriate justification (citing prior work on glutamate response location), and the technical complexity explanation (C103) is plausible given the multi-step immunofluorescence protocol. These represent appropriate acknowledgment of methodological limitations.

results.result: Homeostatic synaptic plasticity is impaired in Rab3a−/− and Rab3a Earlybird mutant cortical cultures. TTX treatment increased mEPSC amplitude in wild-type cultures (13.9 ± 0.7 to 18.2 ± 0.9 pA), but not in Rab3a−/− cultures (13.6 ± 0.1 vs. 14.3 ± 0.6 pA) or Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures (15.1 ± 1.0 vs. 14.6 ± 1.1 pA).
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this as the major finding of the study. Reviewer 1 states 'The major finding - impaired homeostatic up-scaling after TTX treatment in Rab3A KO and Rab3 earlybird mutant neurons - is supported by data of high quality.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'The authors clearly demonstrate the Rab3A plays a role in HSP at excitatory synapses, with substantially less plasticity occurring in the Rab3A KO neurons.'

results.result: Baseline mEPSC amplitude is elevated in Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures compared to wild-type (15.1 ± 1.0 pA vs. 11.0 ± 0.7 pA, p = 0.04), consistent with findings at the NMJ.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges this finding, noting 'There is also no apparent HSP in the Earlybird Rab3A mutation, although baseline synaptic strength is already elevated.' The reviewers discuss this as potentially representing occlusion but do not challenge the data itself.

results.result: The TTX-induced increase in mEPSC amplitude does not depend on Ca2+-permeable receptors, as NASPM application did not reverse the TTX effect on amplitude (before NASPM: CON 12.9 ± 3.5 pA, TTX 17.5 ± 3.1 pA; after NASPM: CON 11.9 ± 2.6 pA, TTX 16.1 ± 3.5 pA).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 challenges this interpretation, noting 'the amplitude data show a strong trend towards smaller amplitude following NASPM treatment (Fig 3B). The p value for both control and TTX neurons was 0.08 - it is very difficult to argue that there is no effect.' The reviewer suggests heterogeneity in receptor composition may complicate the interpretation.

results.result: NASPM reduced mEPSC frequency, with a greater reduction after TTX treatment, suggesting activity blockade promotes synaptic sites containing only Ca2+-permeable receptors that do not contribute to amplitude increases.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 questions the interpretation, stating 'there is a strong frequency effect that is unclear in origin' and suggests alternative explanations including 'pre-synaptic NASPM-sensitive receptors that influence release probability.' The mechanism remains unclear despite the data.

results.result: GluA2 receptor cluster size showed a trend toward increase after TTX (18.1%) similar in magnitude to mEPSC amplitude increase (19.7%), but did not reach statistical significance. No trend was observed in Rab3a−/− cultures.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers identify this as a critical weakness. Reviewer 1 states 'The data on GluA2 modulation after TTX incubation are likely statistically underpowered and do not allow drawing solid conclusions, such as GluA2-independent mechanisms of up-scaling.' Reviewer 2 questions whether 'it is impossible to determine if Rab3A is involved at all' and notes this 'question has not been answered.' Reviewer 3 states 'it remains difficult to distinguish if the apparent difference in imaging and electrophysiology is a methodological issue rather than a biological one.'

results.result: VGLUT1 immunofluorescence was not increased after activity blockade in wild-type or Rab3a−/− cultures, providing no evidence for increased glutamate transporter levels contributing to homeostatic plasticity.
results.evaluation: This negative result is not challenged by reviewers and is consistent with previous literature cited by the authors. The finding is accepted as ruling out one potential presynaptic mechanism.

results.result: Rab3a acts in neurons rather than glia. mEPSC amplitudes increased when Rab3a was present in neurons (WT on WT: CON 13.3 ± 0.5 pA, TTX 16.7 ± 1.2 pA; WT on KO: CON 13.3 ± 1.0 pA, TTX 18.8 ± 1.4 pA), but not when present only in glia (KO on WT: CON 15.2 ± 1.1 pA, TTX 16.9 ± 0.7 pA).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'The authors have solid data showing that Rab3A is unlikely to be active in astrocytes.' However, Reviewer 3 also notes 'The section on TNF is a bit odd. The data on the astrocyte deletion of Rab3A only argues that Rab3A is unlikely to regulate TNF release. But it could easily be downstream of the neuronal TNF receptor.'

results.result: Loss of Rab3a in glia did not disrupt homeostatic plasticity, suggesting Rab3a-dependent homeostatic increase is unlikely via the astrocytic-TNFα pathway, and may involve a non-TNFα mechanism.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly challenges this interpretation: 'The section on TNF is a bit odd. The data on the astrocyte deletion of Rab3A only argues that Rab3A is unlikely to regulate TNF release. But it could easily be downstream of the neuronal TNF receptor. Without any data addressing the TNF response, it seems quite premature to argue that Rab3A is part of a TNF-independent pathway.'

results.result: This is the first demonstration that a protein thought to function presynaptically is required for homeostatic synaptic plasticity of quantal size in central neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly challenges this claim: 'The section title (line 506-7) declaring Rab3A as the first presynaptic protein involved in HSP is also premature, as they don't know it is acting pre-synaptically.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'acknowledge that they should restrict their conclusions to the data in the current study' and questions whether interpretations about presynaptic action should be in the abstract.

results.result: The lack of robust increase in receptor levels leaves open the possibility of a presynaptic contributor to quantal size, though the site of Rab3a action (pre- or postsynaptic) cannot be determined without compartment-specific deletion experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'mechanisms observed at a completely different type of synapses cannot be used as an argument for conclusions here' and that 'it is the conclusive data, rather than interpretations that lack concrete evidence, that support ideas and models.' Reviewer 3 notes 'it remains difficult to distinguish if the apparent difference in imaging and electrophysiology is a methodological issue rather than a biological one. Stronger data, especially positive data on changes in release, will be necessary to conclude that pre-synaptic factors are required for HSP.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement. Both evaluations find the core finding of impaired homeostatic plasticity in Rab3a knockout and Earlybird mutants to be well-supported by high-quality electrophysiological data (C4, C5, C20, C21, C24, C26, C29). This is recognized as the major finding by all reviewers.

Strong agreement. Both evaluations support the glial feeder layer experiments (C7, C69, C70, C73, C74, C75) demonstrating neuronal Rab3a requirement. However, peer reviewer notes the TNF pathway interpretation may be premature, as addressed in R8/R12 concordance.

Strong agreement on uncertainty. Both identify the GluA2 immunofluorescence data (C56, C58, C59, C60, C99, C100, C101) as statistically underpowered and inconclusive. OpenEval notes high variability and lack of significance (p=0.21); peer reviewers emphasize this as a critical weakness preventing conclusions about receptor mechanisms.

Agreement on the data. Both acknowledge the elevated baseline in Rab3aEbd/Ebd cultures (C31, C118) as a documented finding. Peer reviewers discuss potential occlusion interpretation but do not challenge the data quality.

Agreement. Both evaluations accept the negative VGLUT1 results (C61, C62, C63, C90, C92) as ruling out this presynaptic mechanism. The finding is consistent with prior literature and appropriately interpreted.

Disagreement on interpretation. OpenEval finds the NASPM data (C36, C37, C38, C98) supports excluding Ca2+-permeable receptors with appropriate paired design. Peer reviewer challenges this, noting p=0.08 shows strong trend and argues it's difficult to claim no effect, suggesting receptor heterogeneity complicates interpretation.

Agreement on uncertainty. Both evaluations find the NASPM frequency effect mechanism (C41, C42) unclear and speculative. Peer reviewer suggests alternative explanations including presynaptic NASPM-sensitive receptors affecting release probability.

Disagreement. OpenEval finds the TNF pathway argument (C115, C117) logically sound based on glial feeder layer data. Peer reviewer explicitly challenges this as premature, noting Rab3a could act downstream of neuronal TNF receptor and that data only rule out Rab3a in TNF release, not TNF response.

Strong disagreement. OpenEval rates novelty claims (C8, C127) as uncertain due to unclear mechanism. Peer reviewers rate as unsupported, directly challenging the claim that Rab3a is the first presynaptic protein in HSP since the data don't establish presynaptic action.

Partial agreement on uncertainty. OpenEval supports the authors' acknowledgment of limitations and multiple interpretations (C107, C108, C110) as appropriate scientific caution. Peer reviewers are more critical, stating NMJ mechanisms cannot support conclusions here and that stronger positive data on release changes are needed to conclude presynaptic involvement.

OpenEval evaluates competing interpretations of the Earlybird phenotype (C119-C124) as uncertain, noting both occlusion and mimicry hypotheses are speculative. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though peer R2 acknowledges the elevated baseline finding.

Overlap on speculation about mechanisms. OpenEval explicitly marks presynaptic quantum change interpretations (C82, C88, C97) as speculative. Peer reviewers similarly critique reliance on NMJ data for cortical conclusions (C82 appears in both), emphasizing need for direct evidence.

OpenEval identifies frequency changes (C22, C23, C27, C28) as uncertain due to lack of significance (p=0.09), outliers, and baseline differences. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found for these frequency-related claims.
OpenEval supports the documentation of genetic background differences (C25) as appropriate methodological transparency. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval rates alternative analysis treating synapses as independent (C104-C106) as uncertain and methodologically questionable, noting authors appropriately didn't use it as primary analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports methodological details for imaging experiments (C45, C46, C47, C51) as well-documented with appropriate controls. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval supports documentation of culture-to-culture variability in receptor measurements (C52-C55) as transparent reporting of key limitation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this variability is central to peer concerns in R5.
OpenEval supports reporting of baseline differences in glial feeder experiments (C71, C72) with appropriate statistics. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval supports explanations for observed variability in imaging (C102, C103) as appropriate acknowledgment of methodological limitations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
